_about: Short grammar notes for function words, shown when the word is introduced and from its word card. Key: characters|numeric pinyin (as in content/data/words.json). Written for this app; examples are recorded with Azure as g-<n>. Notes give examples in pinyin (characters only where they tell same-sounding words apart).

notes.title: Done, or now different
notes.note: After a verb, le says the action is done: wǒ chīle, I've eaten. At the end of a sentence it says something has changed or is now the case: xià yǔ le, it's raining now.

notes.title: Linking a description to a noun
notes.note: Put de after a person or a description to link it to the noun that follows, like English 's: wǒ de péngyou, my friend; hěn guì de chē, an expensive car. With close family it's often dropped: wǒ māma.

notes.title: How well something is done
notes.note: Verb + de + description says how an action is done: tā shuō de hěn kuài, he speaks fast. It sounds exactly like the de of wǒ de (的) and of màn man de (地); coming right after a verb is what gives it away.
notes.py: Nǐ Zhōngwén shuō de hěn hǎo.

notes.title: Making a description into -ly
notes.note: Description + de + verb says how someone does something: mànmàn de zǒu, walk slowly. It sounds exactly like the other de's (的, 得); here it comes before the verb.

notes.title: Have ever done
notes.note: Verb + guo means you've had the experience at some point: wǒ qùguo Běijīng, I've been to Beijing. Say you haven't with méi: wǒ méi qùguo.
notes.en: Have you ever had Peking duck?

notes.title: An ongoing state
notes.note: Verb + zhe says an action or its result continues: mén kāizhe, the door is open; zuòzhe, sitting. It also says how something is done: xiàozhe shuō, say with a smile.

notes.title: Doing something to a thing
notes.note: Bǎ puts the object before the verb to stress what happens to it: bǎ mén guānshang, shut the door. The verb then needs something after it, such as a result, le or a place.

notes.title: Passive: done to it (by)
notes.note: Thing + bèi + (who did it) + verb: something happened to it, often something unwelcome: wǒ de shǒujī bèi tōu le, my phone was stolen.
notes.py: Wǒ de zìxíngchē bèi tōu le.

notes.title: Let's…, or …, right?
notes.note: At the end of a sentence, ba makes a soft suggestion (wǒmen zǒu ba, let's go) or checks something you assume (nǐ shì Mǐgé ba? you're Mige, right?).

notes.title: And you? / What about…?
notes.note: After a noun, ne asks about it in the same situation: wǒ hěn hǎo, nǐ ne? I'm fine, and you? At the end of a sentence it can also mark something going on right now.

notes.title: Yes/no questions
notes.note: Add ma to the end of a statement to make a yes/no question. Don't use it with question words like shénme or nǎr: they're questions already.

notes.title: Adding feeling
notes.note: At the end of a sentence, a adds feeling or softens it: hǎo a! sure!; shì a, yes indeed. Its sound blends with the word before it (ya, wa, na).

notes.title: Already, right away, then
notes.note: Before a verb, jiù says something is sooner or easier than expected (tā bā diǎn jiù lái le, he came as early as eight), or means 'then' after an 'if'. Jiù shì means exactly or simply.

notes.title: Not until, only then
notes.note: Before a verb, cái says something is later or harder than expected: tā shí diǎn cái lái, he didn't come until ten. Before a number it means only: cái wǔ kuài. The opposite of jiù.
notes.en: He didn't get up until ten.

notes.title: All, both
notes.note: Dōu goes before the verb and sums up the people or things mentioned before it: wǒmen dōu shì xuésheng, we're all students. With a question word it means every: shéi dōu zhīdào, everyone knows.

notes.title: Still, also, even
notes.note: Before a verb, hái means still (tā hái zài shuìjiào, he's still asleep) or in addition (hái yào yì bēi, one more cup). Hái kěyǐ means not bad.

notes.title: Again (it already happened)
notes.note: Yòu is for a repeat that has already happened: tā yòu lái le, he came again. For a repeat still to come, use zài. Yòu… yòu… means both… and…

notes.title: Again (still to come), then
notes.note: Zài is for a repeat that hasn't happened yet: qǐng zài shuō yí biàn, please say it again; míngtiān zài lái, come again tomorrow. It also means and then: xiān chī fàn, zài zǒu.

notes.title: Comparing: more … than
notes.note: A bǐ B + adjective: A is more … than B: tā bǐ wǒ gāo, he's taller than me. Don't add hěn; for much more, put duō le after it: tā bǐ wǒ gāo duō le.

notes.title: With, and
notes.note: Gēn + person + verb: do it with them: wǒ gēn māma shuōhuà, I'm talking with Mum. Gēn… yíyàng means the same as.

notes.title: Give; for or to someone
notes.note: As a verb, gěi means give: gěi wǒ, give me. Before another verb it means for or to someone: gěi tā dǎ diànhuà, call her.
notes.py: Wǒ wǎnshang gěi nǐ dǎ diànhuà.

notes.title: Right; towards
notes.note: On its own, duì means right, correct: duì! Before a person or thing it means towards or to: tā duì wǒ hěn hǎo, he's very good to me.

notes.title: Let, make someone do
notes.note: A ràng B + verb: A lets or has B do something: māma ràng wǒ zǎo diǎnr huí jiā, Mum wants me home early. Ràng wǒ… means let me…

notes.title: Also, too
notes.note: Yě always goes before the verb, never at the end like English too: wǒ yě shì xuésheng, I'm a student too.

notes.title: Very (often just linking)
notes.note: An adjective that describes something usually needs hěn in front: wǒ hěn hǎo, I'm fine. Here hěn often doesn't really mean very; without it the sentence sounds like a comparison.

notes.title: At; in the middle of doing
notes.note: Before a place, zài means at or in: wǒ zài jiā, I'm at home. Before a verb it means doing it right now: wǒ zài chī fàn, I'm eating.

notes.title: Didn't, haven't; don't have
notes.note: Méi says something didn't happen (wǒ méi qù, I didn't go) and negates yǒu (méiyǒu qián, have no money). For habits, plans and shì, use bù.

notes.title: Not
notes.note: Bù negates the present, the future, habits and adjectives: wǒ bú qù, I'm not going. Before a 4th tone it's said bú: bú shì.

notes.title: Can (a learned skill); will
notes.note: Huì + verb means know how to (wǒ huì yóuyǒng, I can swim) or will probably (míngtiān huì xià yǔ, it'll rain tomorrow). For being able or allowed right now, use néng.

notes.title: Can (able or allowed)
notes.note: Néng + verb means able to in this situation, or allowed: wǒ míngtiān bù néng lái, I can't come tomorrow. For a learned skill, use huì.

notes.title: May, can (allowed)
notes.note: Kěyǐ + verb says something is allowed or possible: wǒ kěyǐ jìnlai ma? may I come in? Kěyǐ on its own means that's fine.

notes.title: Want; going to; need to
notes.note: Yào + noun means want: wǒ yào yì bēi chá. Yào + verb means going to or need to: wǒ yào zǒu le, I have to go now. Bú yào means don't.
notes.en: I'd like a cup of tea.

notes.title: To be (between nouns)
notes.note: Shì links two nouns: wǒ shì Dānmài rén, I'm Danish. It isn't used before an adjective: say wǒ hěn gāo, not wǒ shì gāo.

notes.title: Because (…so)
notes.note: Yīnwèi gives the reason first; suǒyǐ can introduce the result: yīnwèi xià yǔ, suǒyǐ wǒ méi qù. Either half can stand alone.
notes.py: Yīnwèi xià yǔ, wǒ méi qù.
notes.en: Because it rained, I didn't go.

notes.title: Although (…but)
notes.note: Suīrán is usually paired with dànshì or kěshì in the second half, unlike English, which uses only one: suīrán hěn lèi, dànshì hěn gāoxìng.
notes.zh: 虽然很累，但是我很高兴。
notes.py: Suīrán hěn lèi, dànshì wǒ hěn gāoxìng.

notes.title: And (between nouns)
notes.note: Hé joins nouns: wǒ hé tā, she and I. It doesn't join sentences or verbs; for those, just put them side by side or use yě, hái or ránhòu.
notes.py: Wǒ hé tā dōu shì xuésheng.
notes.en: She and I are both students.

notes.title: Or (in questions); still
notes.note: In a question, háishi means or: nǐ hē chá háishi kāfēi? tea or coffee? In statements, use huòzhě for or. Háishi can also mean still, or had better.
notes.en: Do you drink tea or coffee?

notes.title: Or (in statements)
notes.note: Huòzhě means or in a statement: jīntiān huòzhě míngtiān, today or tomorrow. In a question asking someone to choose, use háishi.

notes.title: From
notes.note: Cóng + place or time + verb: from: wǒ cóng Dānmài lái, I come from Denmark. Cóng… dào… means from… to…
notes.py: Wǒ cóng bā diǎn dào wǔ diǎn shàngbān.
notes.en: I work from eight to five.

notes.title: Distance from
notes.note: A lí B + yuǎn/jìn says how far A is from B: wǒ jiā lí gōngsī hěn jìn, my home is close to work.
notes.py: Wǒ jiā lí gōngsī hěn jìn.
notes.en: My home is close to work.

notes.title: Already
notes.note: Yǐjīng goes before the verb, usually with le at the end: tā yǐjīng zǒu le, he's already left.

notes.title: In the middle of doing
notes.note: Zhèngzài + verb says an action is going on right now, often with ne at the end: wǒ zhèngzài zuò fàn ne, I'm cooking right now.

notes.title: Too; so
notes.note: Tài + adjective usually comes with le: tài guì le, too expensive; tài hǎo le, great! Bú tài means not very: bú tài hǎo.

notes.title: Most
notes.note: Zuì + adjective or verb means the most: zuì hǎo, the best; wǒ zuì xǐhuan, my favourite.

notes.title: Only
notes.note: Zhǐ goes before the verb: wǒ zhǐ yǒu yí ge, I only have one.
notes.py: Wǒ zhǐ huì shuō yìdiǎnr Zhōngwén.
notes.en: I only speak a little Chinese.

notes.title: The more…, the more…
notes.note: Yuè A yuè B: the more A, the more B. Yuè lái yuè hǎo means better and better.
notes.py: Nǐ de Zhōngwén yuè lái yuè hǎo le.
notes.en: Your Chinese is getting better and better.

notes.title: If
notes.note: Rúguǒ starts the condition; the result often has jiù: rúguǒ xià yǔ, wǒ jiù bú qù le, if it rains, I won't go.
notes.py: Rúguǒ xià yǔ, wǒ jiù bú qù le.
notes.en: If it rains, I won't go.

notes.title: First (…then)
notes.note: Xiān + verb means do it first; the next step often has zài or ránhòu: xiān chī fàn, zài zǒu.
notes.zh: 我们先吃饭，然后去公园。
notes.py: Wǒmen xiān chī fàn, ránhòu qù gōngyuán.
notes.en: Let's eat first, then go to the park.

notes.title: Plural for people
notes.note: Men makes pronouns and people plural: wǒmen, we; péngyoumen, friends. It isn't used with numbers: sān ge péngyou, not sān ge péngyoumen.

notes.title: The everyday measure word
notes.note: Between a number (or zhè/nà) and a noun you need a measure word; ge is the all-rounder: yí ge rén, zhège wèntí.
